Hi Hannah,

We are doing a quick billing reconciliation for the month and a couple of items are unclear to our finance team: how Redwood accounts for small, interleaved calls (our product does many tiny assistant queries across the same conversation id) and how minimums / rounding apply.

Two specific asks:
1) If we make 30 short calls (200–400 tokens each) that are interleaved across the same conversation id over 8 hours, does Redwood round each call individually or aggregate before applying the billing quantum/minimum?
2) If a single customer has very low daily traffic, what prevents a near-zero invoice line from appearing (is there a per-day or per-invoice floor)?

I attached a sample invoice line and our raw usage export for October to help. Can you share the exact rules and a short worked example so we can map to our internal forecasting model?

Hi all — attaching the billing rule summary below and two worked examples based on Taylor's numbers. Short summary first, then details.

Executive summary (current platform behavior):
- Raw token counting: we count input + output tokens per request precisely.
- Metering quantum: before pricing is applied we apply a per-request rounding quantum of 25 tokens (round up).
- Fallthrough aggregation: requests that share the same conversation_id are aggregated into a single metering bucket if they occur within a 10-minute fallthrough window; when aggregated we sum raw tokens first, then apply a single 25-token upward rounding to the bucket (reduces rounding overhead).
- Microfloor for invoice noise: to avoid sub-dollar invoice noise, we apply a per-customer microfloor of 250 billed tokens per 24-hour UTC day; any billed tokens below that threshold are carried as residual credit toward the next day (i.e., not invoiced separately). Committed deals may override this behavior per contract.
- KV/prefix reuse credit: when the runtime serves tokens from a warmed KV cache for an identical prefix within the same conversation, we apply a 50% reuse credit on those output tokens for the first reuse event and a 75% credit for subsequent reuses within the same billing window.

Worked example A — 30 interleaved short calls, same conversation_id, gaps under 10 minutes:
- Each call raw tokens: average 320 tokens
- Because gaps < 10 min, fallthrough aggregation groups the 30 calls into a single bucket: total raw tokens = 30 * 320 = 9,600 tokens
- Apply single quantum rounding (25 tokens) to bucket: round up 9,600 to next multiple of 25 = 9,600 (already multiple)
- Billed tokens = 9,600 (so per-request rounding overhead avoided).

Worked example B — 30 short calls, same conversation_id, gaps > 10 minutes so buckets split into 5 buckets of 6 calls each:
- One bucket raw = 6 * 320 = 1,920 tokens -> round to nearest 25 up = 1,925 billed tokens per bucket
- 5 buckets -> billed tokens = 5 * 1,925 = 9,625 tokens
- Note: the extra 25 tokens per bucket is rounding overhead compared to aggregate.

Microfloor example (low-volume customer):
- If a customer accrues 180 billed tokens in UTC day X (after quanta rounding), that is <250 microfloor. We will not generate a separate invoice line for that day; instead we carry the 70-token shortfall as a credit into day X+1. If day X+1 brings total billed tokens >=250, we invoice normally and apply the carried credit. This prevents small invoice lines.

Other notes:
- Streaming calls: we bill the same way — streaming just reports tokens as they are emitted; each streaming session's tokens are counted toward the request and follow the same quantum/aggregation semantics.
- Committed or Dedicated customers: contracts can change the quantum and microfloor (commonly increased quanta to 100 tokens for enterprise plans to simplify accounting). If PayWell has a committed SKU we should surface that in the SOW.

If you'd like, I can produce a short CSV showing your exported rows transformed into "billed_token" arithmetic so your finance team can reconcile line-by-line.

Regards,
Kimberly Park
Billing & Pricing, Redwood Inference
